---
applyTo: "spec/**/*.rb"
---

# Fake clients

- Use a fake client in `spec/support` only when neither WebMock nor the SDK's own stubs can reach the client, e.g. a socket client with no stubs such as the `mqtt` gem. In request, feature, job and service specs, you MUST NOT stub the gem's client class or the service around it, e.g. `instance_double(MQTT::Client)` or `allow(PostNotifier).to receive(:default)`.
- Block the gem's real connections for every spec in a `before` hook in its support file, with a message that names the helpers to use, e.g. `config.before { allow(MQTT::Client).to receive(:connect).and_raise("Use stub_mqtt_connection or stub_mqtt_message") }` in `spec/support/mqtt.rb`, because `WebMock.disable_net_connect!` doesn't cover sockets.
- Define one fake in the gem's support file, named `Fake` then the client's class, e.g. `FakeMqttClient` in `spec/support/mqtt.rb`. Give it only the methods the app calls, with the real client's parameter names, even for parameters it ignores, e.g. `def disconnect(send_msg = true)`. Record each outbound call, e.g. each published message and subscribed topic.
- Give a blocking read a defined end, so a spec never waits on a socket. With a block, yield every queued message in order, then return. Without a block, return the next message. Raise only when nothing was queued, e.g. `raise "No MQTT message queued. Add one with stub_mqtt_message" if queued_messages.empty?` at the top of `FakeMqttClient#get`.
- Give the fake its own spec outside `spec/support`, with one example for each method in `described_class.public_instance_methods(false)`, other than the readers for its recorded calls and queue, which checks that the real client has the same parameters, e.g. `expect(described_class.instance_method(name).parameters).to eq(MQTT::Client.instance_method(name).parameters)` in `spec/fakes/fake_mqtt_client_spec.rb`.
- In the fake's spec, also check the fake's own behaviour: queued messages come back in order, subscribed topics are recorded, and reading with nothing queued raises, e.g. `expect { client.get }.to raise_error(/No MQTT message queued/)`.
- Return the fake from the gem's connect method, not from the service, so the service's own code runs, e.g. its pool, e.g. `allow(MQTT::Client).to receive(:connect).and_return(fake_mqtt_client)` in `stub_mqtt_connection`.
- Put the fake's stubs in a helper module in the gem's support file, with one `stub_` method for each inbound message or failure the specs need, named after the gem, the message and the method it stubs, e.g. `stub_mqtt_message(topic, payload)` and `stub_mqtt_publish_failure` in `MqttHelpers`, with `stub_mqtt_connection_failure` for `MQTT::Client.connect` and `stub_mqtt_reconnect_failure` for `FakeMqttClient#connect`. You MUST NOT call `allow` on the fake in a spec. Add a helper instead.
- End every `stub_` helper by returning the fake, e.g. `fake_mqtt_client` on its last line, and keep it in a local variable in the spec, e.g. `mqtt_client = stub_mqtt_publish_failure`.
- In a failure helper, raise the error the real method raises, read from the gem's source. That is usually the gem's own error, e.g. `MQTT::Exception` from `publish`, but sometimes the socket's, e.g. `Errno::EPIPE` from `disconnect`. When the default isn't the gem's own error, say why in a comment above the helper.
- Give each failure helper an `error` argument, with the real method's error as its default, e.g. `def stub_mqtt_connection_failure(error = MQTT::Exception.new("Connection refused"))`, called as `stub_mqtt_connection_failure(Errno::ECONNREFUSED)`.
- Queue one more message on each call to a message helper. Queue the messages for each run just before it, because a run drains the queue, e.g. call `stub_mqtt_message` again before the second `RecordPostReadsJob.perform_now`.
- Build each message a spec queues as a Ruby hash with `to_json`, e.g. `stub_mqtt_message("posts/#{post.id}/read", { "device" => "ios" }.to_json)`. You MUST NOT hand-escape JSON in a string. When you convert a string to a hash, check that both parse to the same JSON, e.g. `"3.1"` stays a string.
- Check each outbound call with a `have_` matcher on the fake, named after the verb, the gem and the message, e.g. `have_published_mqtt_message` and `have_reconnected_mqtt_client`. Give it the call's arguments, with keywords for the parts to check, matched like `have_requested`, e.g. `matcher :have_published_mqtt_message do |topic, **options|`.
- Parse the payload as JSON inside the matcher unless the spec passes a string. Check the exact string in the service's own spec, e.g. `payload: { title: "Hello World", id: post.id }.to_json`, and only the parts the spec is about elsewhere, e.g. `expect(mqtt_client).to have_published_mqtt_message("posts/#{post.id}/published", payload: a_hash_including("title" => "Hello World"))`.
- Give each matcher a `failure_message` that lists every message the fake recorded.
- Match a value the app generates by its format in request, job and feature specs, e.g. `"message_id" => a_string_matching(/\A\h{8}-\h{4}-\h{4}-\h{4}-\h{12}\z/)` for a UUID. Check that two fields hold the same value only in the service's own spec, where the spec passes the value in.
- Give each spec a new fake, and clear the service's cached connections after each spec, so no spec gets the last spec's client, e.g. `config.after { PostNotifier.const_get(:POOLS).clear }`.
- Test reconnecting and error handling with the fake and its failure helpers, e.g. `stub_mqtt_reconnect_failure(Errno::ECONNREFUSED)`. Test what depends on timing or the wire, e.g. keepalive timeouts and TLS, in one spec for the service's connection code against a real broker or the gem's in-process server, e.g. `MQTT::FakeServer`. You MUST NOT test what the app does over a real socket.
